clue.text: Will he make it wet for the sinners left (presumably) outside?

definitions.text: Will he make it wet for the sinners left (presumably) outside?

parts.words: Will he make it wet for the sinners left (presumably) outside?
parts.note: the saint whose feast on 15 July, legend says, brings forty days of rain if it is wet; the sinners shut out of heaven would be the ones rained on

explanation.surface: A question about who soaks the wicked left standing outside the pearly gates.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue's 'inners' is an OCR slip; the page prints 'sinners'. English weather lore says rain on St Swithin's Day (15 July) means forty more wet days.
explanation.definitionFit: Folklore makes this saint the patron of a long rainy spell, so he is the one blamed for wetting anyone left outdoors.

clue.text: Extend the sentence

definitions.meaning: slang for a term in prison

explanation.surface: A judge lengthening a prison term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sentence' is a prison term, not a line of words; criminal slang calls a jail term a stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen something is to draw it out, and criminal slang calls a jail term by the same word.

clue.text: Little demon up to get a hundred lines?

parts.note: an imp is a small devil

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word to is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A naughty child likely to be set lines as punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses TO in this down clue. An impot (from imposition) is a school punishment of writing out lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for imposition, it is the British school penalty of copying out many lines.

clue.text: Saucy as hell!

definitions.meaning: the word as if made from tartare sauce
belonging to Tartarus, the underworld of Greek myth

explanation.surface: An exclamation that something is outrageously cheeky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy' plays on tartare sauce rather than cheek; the real sense is of Tartarus, the Greek infernal pit.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartarus was the deepest pit of the Greek underworld, so its adjective means hellish, while the sound recalls tartare sauce.

clue.text: Stop order to the drink dispenser

definitions.text: Stop order to the drink dispenser

parts.words: Stop order to the drink dispenser
parts.note: a host pouring asks you to say this word ... your glass is full enough

explanation.surface: An instruction to a barman to stop pouring.
explanation.walkthrough: A host pouring a drink says 'Say ...', and you call out this word when you have enough.
explanation.definitionFit: The polite call to halt the pouring of a drink is the word answering 'Say ...'.

clue.text: Short week-end upset with mental disorder in Commonwealth State

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, so it is read from the bottom

parts.note: Saturday, the end of the week, shortened to Sat
mania is a mental disorder of excess excitement

explanation.surface: Someone disturbed by a cut weekend and a breakdown, somewhere in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns SAT into TAS. The Commonwealth here is the Commonwealth of Australia, whose island state is Tasmania.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasmania is the island state of the Commonwealth of Australia.

clue.text: Decorative insertion in song

parts.note: a lay is an old word for a ballad or song

explanation.surface: An ornamental flourish added to a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Inlaid work sets pieces of wood, stone or metal into a surface as ornament.

clue.text: When kiddies get destructive beware of this

definitions.text: When kiddies get destructive beware of this

parts.words: When kiddies get destructive beware of this
parts.note: split as the age at which children start smashing things, which is also the damage itself

explanation.surface: A parent's warning about toddlers who smash things.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as BREAK AGE, the stage of childhood when things get smashed; as one word it is the smashing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Broken items are what destructive children leave behind, and split, it is the age when they break things.

clue.text: Bleed a crazy college official

indicators.note: crazy says the letters of these two words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A demented university officer being bled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' rearranges the six letters of BLEED A.
explanation.definitionFit: A beadle is a ceremonial officer at some universities and colleges, carrying a mace in processions.

clue.text: It's news to us that they deliver daily

definitions.text: It's news to us that they deliver daily

parts.words: It's news to us that they deliver daily
parts.note: read as milkmen or postmen delivering, but the delivery is news itself, handed in every day by journalists

explanation.surface: Someone surprised to learn which tradesmen call every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's news to us' sounds like surprise; read literally, what they deliver daily is the news.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalists file stories every day, so the news is what these writers hand over.

clue.text: Whereat one is free

parts.note: split 'whereat' into 'where at': the word following 'at' in the phrase meaning free, like an escaped prisoner

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned legal phrase about the moment of release.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whereat' is an archaic connective, but split it into 'where at': one is free when 'at' this word, as in a convict who is still at large.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner at large is at liberty, so this word is where 'at' leaves you free.

clue.text: It's sent back twice to an artist

indicators.note: twice says the reversed piece appears two times in a row
sent back says the word It is read from end to start

parts.note: the possessive 's adds nothing; the word is It

explanation.surface: Something returned to a painter two times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns IT into TI, and 'twice' repeats it: TITI, then AN as written. Titian was the Venetian Renaissance painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Titian, the Venetian master of the sixteenth century, is a celebrated painter.

clue.text: The queen is to disembark in state

parts.note: Mary was the name of several English and Scottish queens
to disembark is to land from a ship

explanation.surface: A monarch about to step off a ship on arrival in a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Maryland is one of the United States, named after Queen Henrietta Maria.

clue.text: Reached half-score and must hurry

parts.note: someone who has reached an age 'has' it, so reached gives has
a score is twenty, so half of one is ten

explanation.surface: A runner halfway through a count of twenty told to get a move on.
explanation.walkthrough: A score is twenty, so half a score is TEN; 'has ten' is having reached that number.
explanation.definitionFit: To hurry and to speed up are synonyms, so 'must hurry' is a call to go faster.

clue.text: The security of a certain land-salient

parts.note: certain and sure are synonyms
a ness is a headland, land jutting out into the sea

explanation.surface: Defence of a promontory that sticks out into enemy ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salient' sounds military, but a land-salient is a headland, a NESS as in Loch Ness or Dungeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Security in the sense of confidence or certainty is a synonym.

clue.text: Funny Harry's sister has to give the facts wrong

definitions.meaning: Harry Tate was a famous music-hall comedian

explanation.surface: A comedian's sibling who keeps garbling the details.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Tate was a British music-hall comic of the early twentieth century; an unmarried sister would be addressed as Miss Tate.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is a title and surname for a comic's sister; as one, it means to report inaccurately.

clue.text: These persons are not so talkative

definitions.text: These persons are not so talkative

parts.words: These persons are not so talkative
parts.note: people with no nationality; split, the word means saying less, since to state is to say

explanation.surface: A remark about people who keep quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as STATE LESS it means saying less; as one word it describes people with no nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: People with no citizenship anywhere are without a country, and to state is to speak, so the split reads as speaking less.

clue.text: Revealing how to spin yarn

parts.note: to spin a story is to tell it
a yarn is a story or tale

explanation.surface: A guide to storytelling that gives the game away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spin yarn' sounds like spinning wool; a yarn is a story, and to spin one is to tell it.
explanation.definitionFit: A telltale sign gives something away, so the adjective means revealing.

clue.text: A jumper for a dog !

definitions.meaning: one who leaps, from spring meaning jump

explanation.surface: A clothing pun on a sweater bought for a pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' suggests the British word for a sweater, as if knitwear for a dog; it is one who leaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that leaps springs, and the springer spaniel is a gundog breed named for flushing game.

clue.text: Tom the Woodcutter

explanation.surface: A named woodcutter, as in a fairy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Twain's boy hero is Tom Sawyer; a sawyer is someone who saws wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain's hero bears the surname, and the common noun means one who saws timber.

clue.text: Rush madly into a profession

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to hurtle along out of control
as a noun, a working life or occupation

explanation.surface: Someone diving headlong into a line of work.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to hurtle wildly; as a noun it is the course of a working life.

clue.text: Screen with red centre and unusual rose edging

indicators.note: centre puts the word red at the middle of the other piece
edging means the jumbled letters border the word red on both sides
unusual signals that the letters of rose are rearranged

explanation.surface: A partition with a red middle and an odd rose border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' turns ROSE into REOS, and 'edging' with 'centre' puts RED in the middle: RE-RED-OS. A reredos is the ornamental screen behind an altar.
explanation.definitionFit: A reredos is the decorated screen or panel behind a church altar.

clue.text: What's unexpectedly left after the mistral?

definitions.text: What's unexpectedly left after the mistral?

parts.words: What's unexpectedly left after the mistral?
parts.note: fruit blown down by a strong wind such as the mistral, which also means an unexpected gain

explanation.surface: A question about what remains once the fierce wind of southern France has blown through.
explanation.walkthrough: The mistral is a strong wind of southern France; the fruit it knocks from trees is the literal sense, and a sudden piece of luck the figurative one.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit brought down by a gale lies free for the taking, hence a sudden unearned gain.

clue.text: Sweet cook

definitions.meaning: a soft confection of sugar, butter and milk
to fiddle or falsify, as in cooking the books

explanation.surface: A nice person who prepares food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cook' here is to falsify, as in cooking the books, not to prepare food.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a soft sugary confection, and to falsify figures is to fiddle them.

clue.text: He has no choice, poor chap

definitions.meaning: from the proverb that such people cannot be choosers
a pauper who asks for alms

explanation.surface: Pity for a man left without options.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb runs 'beggars can't be choosers'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb denies the needy any choosing, and a mendicant is a poor man asking for money.

clue.text: Gray end of a glorious path

definitions.text: Gray end of a glorious path

parts.words: Gray end of a glorious path
parts.note: Thomas Gray's Elegy says the paths of glory lead to this place

explanation.surface: A dull ending to a splendid road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gray' looks like a colour but is the poet Thomas Gray, whose Elegy says 'The paths of glory lead but to the grave'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's Elegy says glory leads only to burial, so the tomb is the end of that path.

clue.text: Measures the young steer up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up turns the word for a young steer to read from the bottom

parts.note: a stot is a young bullock or steer

explanation.surface: A guide to steering children, or a young ox being sized up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses STOT, a dialect word for a young steer. 'the young' also defines the answer as small children.
explanation.definitionFit: Small drinks of spirits are poured as tots, little measures.

clue.text: Relaxed point as editor

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor making a point with less tension.
explanation.definitionFit: Slackened and loosened are synonyms of the definition, a past tense verb as is the answer.

clue.text: A verbal warning given of course in advance

parts.note: golfers shout this word to warn others on the course of an incoming ball
spoken aloud, put into words, so said

explanation.surface: A spoken caution delivered well ahead of time, as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally', but it is a golf course, where the shout of warning is FORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mentioned earlier in a document has been stated before, that is, in advance of what follows.

clue.text: Stars take the road past Finsbury Park

definitions.meaning: the Pleiades, a cluster of stars named after seven mythical sisters
a road in north London running beside the park of that name

explanation.surface: Celebrities heading down a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: The held 'Stairs' is an OCR slip; the page prints 'Stars'. Seven Sisters Road runs from Holloway past Finsbury Park in north London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pleiades are the star cluster of Greek myth's seven daughters of Atlas, and a north London road and district bear that name.
